title: Audit Report for Self-Help Chatbot
author: Keith Porcaro · Carmela D'Antuono · Wilson Jeter · Bridgett Kohno · Alexander McElya · Nikolas Osorio · Melinda Xiong · Demi Yang

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The audit accepts the cluster’s use-context-specific, selective-deployment proposition and materially extends it with a detailed real-world evaluation of a public-facing court chatbot. Its findings show that usefulness varies by task and depends on actionability, context retention, authoritative content, interface design, maintenance, verification and continuing human oversight, while expressly avoiding generalisation from one product to LLMs overall.
qs: This audit assesses a product, not a model.
At the same time, public-facing court resources require continued attention to accuracy, clarity, accountability, human oversight, and technical improvement.

st.t: Justice chatbots: Actionable help exceeds correct information
st.an: The audit directly supports the cluster’s proposition that access-to-justice value depends on actionable procedural help, not merely correct information. It documents answers that lacked links, forms or next steps, alongside substantial form-request failures, while also recognising successful performance on some tasks and limits in what session data can establish.
qs: In general, sessions with this label have correct information, but are missing links, references to specific forms, or other information that would help a user advance their problem.
No Impact: 92 sessions  In these sessions, users requested a particular form and the bot did not provide a responsive answer.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The audit supports the cluster’s implementation-focused proposition by showing that conversational access alone does not ensure reliable legal assistance. Its observed clarification and relevance failures reinforce the need for task-specific evaluation, routing safeguards and escalation, while its limited red-team results caution against broad claims of automated tailored advice.
qs: (e.g., a user asks about custody, but does not clarify whether they are married to the other parent.)  The bot rarely asks for clarification of unclear chats, although this appears to have improved with more recent foundation models.
Here, the bot tends to just respond with the single result in the knowledge base, rather than ensuring that the user's question is on-book.

mo.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
Cheaper assistance: More participation may not yield remedies
Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
Self-representation: Cheaper filings may shift institutional costs

kp.k: Audit evaluates a court product, not LLMs generally
kp.d: The Spring 2026 Duke Law course audit reviewed every session in the supplied 2025 dataset, using manual topic tagging, subject-specific rubrics, session impact labels and open-ended investigation of product issues. Transcript logging began in February 2025. Nearly every session had multiple reviewers, but the authors acknowledge inter-reader reliability issues, overlapping labels and approximate totals. Updates during the reporting and audit periods, including responses to draft findings, mean some problems may already have been fixed.
qs: This audit assesses a product, not a model.
This audit covers every session in the dataset we were provided.
Because of the overlapping labels, subtotals throughout the report may not add up to 100%.

kp.k: Court chatbot supplements self-help through retrieval-augmented generation
kp.d: Nevada AOC deployed the CiviLaw.Tech chatbot in summer 2024 to help Nevadans obtain family-law information. Its RAG architecture retrieves extracts from two documents—a running adaptation of the Self-Help website and a court directory—for a foundation LLM to generate answers. In the foreword, State Court Administrator Katherine Stocks frames appropriate use as expanding access to public information for self-represented litigants, subject to accuracy, accountability and human oversight, rather than novelty.
qs: In summer 2024, the Nevada Administrative Office of the Courts (AOC) deployed a chatbot for their Self-Help website.
Here, Nevada AOC relies on two documents for their knowledge base: one is a running adaptation of the Self-Help website material, and another is a basic directory of Nevada courts.
Tools designed to support court users should be evaluated not by novelty, but by whether they help people better understand and move through legal processes.

kp.k: Low engagement is confounded by design and measurement
kp.d: The starting dataset contained 1,792 sessions; 54 were likely tests or junk, nine had no bot messages, and 241 duplicate or continued sessions were consolidated into 104. The authors estimate at most 1,601 unique user sessions, not distinct users. Single-message sessions accounted for 1,204 sessions (67.2%). They suspect erased histories after following links contribute to duplicates and abandonment, but lacked individual-user and chatbot-page visit data needed to establish user counts or conversion rates.
qs: In total, we estimate there are at most 1,601 unique sessions from users.
We did not find any broad correlation between number of user messages and the assessed quality of the bot's answers.
We were not provided data on the number of visits to the page that hosts the bot, so we do not have data on user conversion rates.

kp.k: Actionability varies substantially across legal tasks
kp.d: Reported helpful-and-actionable counts included 198 of 374 consolidated non-excluded divorce sessions, 76 of 89 name-change sessions, 44 of 165 custody/paternity sessions, and 21 of 64 guardianship sessions. Fees received 145 helpful-and-actionable labels, including 136 fee-waiver sessions. Counts are not mutually exclusive performance rates: sessions could receive multiple labels. The authors associate strong name-change performance with a relatively straightforward process; elsewhere correct answers frequently lacked links, specific forms or next steps.
qs: The majority of name change sessions were helpful, accurate, and actionable.
Name change is a relatively straightforward process in Nevada, which likely contributes to the answer quality here.
Some prolonged conversations may have multiple impact labels, reflecting the mixed quality of different answers.

kp.k: Rare harmful answers misdirect substantive and procedural choices
kp.d: Harm labels represent reviewers' judgments about likely consequences of following incorrect or misleading instructions, not observed user outcomes. Examples include three divorce sessions, one child-support session suggesting termination of parental rights, three adoption/parental-rights sessions, one annulment session and two appeal sessions. Appeal errors included a typically 30-day deadline for Justice Court appeals and suggesting a power-of-attorney holder could file on another's behalf, which the auditors identified as raising potential unauthorized-practice concerns.
qs: Harm need not be severe: filing the wrong form, pursuing the wrong procedure, or wasting time chasing an unhelpful option all count.
Harmful sessions are rare; we also tried to account for the likelihood that a user would encounter something in the world that would correct the bot's error before the user took an action.
In this session, the user asked how they could terminate child support. The bot suggested that the user terminate their parental rights.

kp.k: Forms retrieval frequently fails users' practical needs
kp.d: In 506 sessions, users sought forms, filing help, or records/case information, with overlapping categories of 308, 132 and 84 respectively. After exclusions and consolidation, the 238 evaluated form-finding sessions received 92 no-impact, 64 marginal-impact, 40 helpful-not-actionable and 58 helpful-and-actionable labels, plus five harmful labels. Recurring failures included defining a requested form instead of supplying it, incorrectly asserting availability, and sending users through generic pages. The bot also failed to point users toward county online records systems in the examples reviewed.
qs: Most commonly, the bot would define the form or surrounding procedure, even when the user explicitly asked for the form.
If the form did not exist, the bot would not tell the user that it didn't exist, and would give a generic or circular answer instead of next steps.
In addition, we did not find examples of the bot pointing users to online records systems that some county courts in Nevada maintain.

kp.k: Ambiguity and context failures produce mismatched legal pathways
kp.d: Across topics, the bot sometimes assumed material facts, procedural stages or case types rather than clarifying them, and failed to retain prior messages. It repeatedly suggested separate custody filings to divorcing parents despite contrary source guidance. In general custody sessions, 15/21 omitted the child's six-month Nevada residence requirement and only 5 of 21 mentioned joint filings. Real sessions and synthetic testing showed that identical or slightly rephrased questions could produce materially different answers; the authors also document occasional successful navigation of intersecting processes.
qs: The bot's answers will sometimes assume that a user is at a random point in the custody process.
Small changes in prompts can yield very different answers.
In rare cases, the bot will ask appropriate follow-up questions before giving an answer.

kp.k: Scope controls reject only some unsupported questions
kp.d: Approximately 270 sessions contained off-book questions, including housing, technical support, debt, criminal matters and traffic cases. The bot appropriately declined about 60% of the time and did better on entirely unrelated topics than on questions superficially related to its knowledge base. The authors propose, without establishing, that a low retrieval relevance cutoff contributes to generic or irrelevant answers. Among 81 unclear sessions, 68 contained broad questions needing clarification; the bot rarely sought it, though the authors observed apparent improvement with more recent foundation models.
qs: About 60% of the time, the bot appropriately declined to answer off-book questions.
Here, it appears that the relevance cutoff in some cases may be too low.
While the majority of these responses are not harmful, few of them are helpful.

kp.k: Limited tests expose porous boundaries around legal advice
kp.d: Small red-team tests found that the bot generally avoided specific fact-tailored guidance but approached advice when comparing scenarios, and could suggest language for narrative sections of petitions. Synthetic tests also showed inconsistent correction of user misconceptions: one answer implied a 16-year-old could become a guardian, whereas rewording elicited the correct age requirement. These are limited product tests, not findings that the system generally engages in unauthorized practice.
qs: In general, the bot mostly avoided giving specific, fact-tailored guidance.
The bot veered closest to advice when asked to compare two situations.
When presented with a slightly different wording, the bot will correctly identify the age requirement to become a guardian.

kp.k: Emergency support depends too heavily on explicit wording
kp.d: The audit found weak emergency-custody guidance and missing knowledge-base material on emergency and ex parte pickup orders despite its presence on the website. The bot recommended 911 for explicit abuse language but inconsistently recognized less explicit dangerous situations, and rarely supplied detailed CPS contact information. In synthetic suicidal-ideation testing, it appeared to crash and returned a generic failure response. The report recommends more specific domestic-violence resources, including Nevada 211, and suicide and mental-health crisis lines.
qs: One area where we did not see improvement in answers over time was emergency custody.
But the bot does not do as well identifying dangerous situations that are less explicit.
In synthetic testing, the bot appears to crash when the user expresses suicidal ideation.

kp.k: Language and interface barriers constrain accessible public service
kp.d: Only 35 sessions, around 2% of the dataset, were in Spanish, compared with nearly one-third of Nevadans speaking a language other than English at home. The authors hypothesize access barriers rather than establish their cause; most website material was English-only. Spanish answer quality varied and no Spanish sessions requested feedback. Other barriers included weak orientation, a robot icon without a text invitation, an unofficial-looking Azure URL, mobile scrolling and overflow problems, and erased conversations after link navigation. Recommendations include clearer orientation, an official domain, new-tab links and short-term history retention.
qs: None of the Spanish-language sessions asked users to submit feedback.
The bot currently lacks any meaningful introductory or descriptive materials.
Opening links in a new tab and retaining conversation history for short period of time would greatly improve the bot's usability.

kp.k: Confidentiality information is absent despite sensitive user disclosures
kp.d: The reviewers counted five sessions containing potential personally identifiable information, excluding likely tests. One user submitted an entire custody order and asked detailed questions across three sessions, which the audit partner identified and redacted. The chatbot did not explain conversation-data handling, confidentiality or the risks of submitting identifying information. Technical indicators suggested Google Analytics use, but the audit explicitly did not assess reidentification risk.
qs: The bot lacks a meaningful confidentiality disclosure.

The bot currently provides no information to users about how their conversation data is handled or whether their data is treated as confidential, nor does it warn users against submitting personally identifiable information to the bot.
Although there are technical indicators that Google Analytics is used on the chatbot site, assessing user reidentification risk is out of scope for this audit.

kp.k: Broken links and opaque citations weaken source checking
kp.d: Of 1,792 sessions, 1,495 contained links; the auditors found 151 unique links, with 46 unique broken links across 97 sessions. Many failures arose from incorrectly written URL text in the knowledge base even where underlying clickable hyperlinks were correct. References sometimes opened isolated pages without adequate context; the authors estimate at least 20% of knowledge-base citations appeared unrelated to the answer. In 351 sessions the bot cited multiple knowledge-base versions, suggesting incomplete replacement of older material rather than necessarily harmful answers.
qs: Of these, 46 unique links across 97 sessions were broken.
We estimate that at least 20% of the knowledge base citations do not appear to have any relationship to the answer.
Finally, in 351 sessions, the bot appeared to cite from multiple versions of the knowledge base in a single session.

kp.k: Integrated information systems may outperform a separate chatbot
kp.d: The authors identify an additional maintenance burden from a secondary knowledge base that is not consistently synchronized with the website and minimally references useful Clark and Washoe County materials. Website search and navigation also had broken results, missing indexed topics and query failures, potentially driving users toward the bot. While full redesign recommendations were outside scope, the report proposes direct retrieval from website materials and cautiously suggests natural-language search returning relevant site results might provide a better experience than separate search and chatbot interfaces.
qs: An enduring challenge with the chatbot is the additional maintenance burden of yet another knowledge base, which remains somewhat isolated from the high-quality resources on the Self-Help website.
A review of historical snapshots of the Self-Help website (via the Internet Archive) suggests that the website and knowledge base are not always updated in sync.

While full recommendations for changes are outside the scope of this audit, a more robustly integrated bot might rely directly on the website materials to power a RAG search, rather than a secondary knowledge base.

kp.k: Official chatbot value and user trust remain research questions
kp.d: A small comparison with GPT, Claude and Gemini found the court chatbot generally briefer and better cited, with more specific official links, while foundation-model answers were more verbose. In one synthetic financial-disclosure question, only one foundation model identified a 2025 law sealing specified records by default. The authors explicitly reject treating this exercise as a generalizable capability study and call for research on whether official court provenance reduces users' inclination to verify AI output.
qs: This should not be considered a generalizable study of frontier AI capabilities with respect to legal questions.
In general, the Self-Help chatbot's answers tended to be briefer but better-cited, with more specific links to official sources.
More research is needed to determine whether users are less likely to verify AI-generated information when it comes from an "official" source, like the court.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Court-provided chatbots can expand access to legal information for self-represented litigants, but this benefit is conditional on appropriate use and continuing oversight.
pts.d: In the foreword, Nevada State Court Administrator Katherine Stocks describes the chatbot as an information-navigation resource rather than a replacement for legal representation. She identifies particular value for people confronting unfamiliar forms, procedures and terminology without legal assistance or outside business hours. This is an institutional statement of potential benefit, not an audit finding that access to justice or case outcomes actually improved.

pts.k: The chatbot sometimes provides actionable procedural help, but usefulness varies substantially by legal topic and by whether answers supply concrete next steps.
pts.d: Porcaro and the audit team report particularly strong performance on relatively straightforward name-change and fee-waiver questions. They label 76 name-change sessions and 145 fee-related sessions helpful and actionable; 136 of the latter concerned fee waivers. They also identify 198 divorce sessions as helpful and actionable. By contrast, many custody, guardianship, forms and court-procedure answers were correct but lacked links or specific steps needed to advance the user's problem. The authors suggest that the relative simplicity of Nevada name changes contributes to performance, and describe one custody/protection-order exchange as improving on the website by explaining how processes intersect. These are assessments of answer usefulness, not measured effects on completed filings or legal outcomes.

pts.k: Incorrect or misapplied chatbot guidance can expose court users to procedural harm, even when the underlying information resembles valid legal material.
pts.d: The audit team calls harmful sessions rare, but identifies examples involving divorce eligibility, child support, adoption, annulment, appeals and service. Examples include suggesting termination of parental rights to end child support; applying domestic adoption information to a foreign-born child despite the website's warning; and supplying an overly long appeal deadline for a justice-court case. Harm is assessed prospectively: it includes filing the wrong form, pursuing the wrong process or wasting time if instructions are followed. The report does not establish that users acted on these answers or suffered actual harm. The authors also report a possible unauthorized-practice concern where the bot suggested a person with power of attorney could file an appeal for someone else.

pts.k: Weak clarification, context retention and scope control limit the reliability of conversational legal self-help.
pts.d: The authors find that the chatbot sometimes ignores previous messages, assumes material facts or the user's procedural stage, and gives substantially different answers to identical or slightly rephrased questions. Approximately 270 sessions contained questions outside the knowledge base; the bot appropriately declined about 60% of the time. It struggled particularly when retrieved material was related to a question but did not actually answer it. The team hypothesizes that an overly permissive retrieval-relevance cutoff contributes to generic or irrelevant answers, rather than claiming to have established the technical cause. They predict that more consistent, appropriate follow-up questions would improve usefulness and rejection of unanswerable requests.

pts.k: Interface and language-access barriers may suppress engagement with court AI, independently of answer quality.
pts.d: The audit estimates at most 1,601 unique user sessions, not individual users, and reports that 67.2% of unconsolidated sessions contained one user message. The authors attribute many duplicate or continued sessions to links opening in the same tab and conversation history disappearing on return. They hypothesize that this frustrates users and suppresses continued use; opening links separately and briefly retaining history are expected to improve usability. They also suggest that limited orientation, an unofficial-looking deployment URL and mobile interface problems hinder use. Only 35 sessions were in Spanish, approximately 2% of the dataset. Drawing partly on demographic context and a Las Vegas survey, the authors regard language barriers as a likely contributor, while acknowledging low overall usage as another possible explanation.

pts.k: Public-facing legal chatbots create safety and confidentiality requirements that this implementation does not consistently meet.
pts.d: The audit team reports that explicit descriptions of harm can trigger emergency recommendations, but less explicit dangerous situations are not consistently recognized. Logged emergency-related exchanges and limited synthetic testing revealed omitted emergency referrals or insufficiently specific resources. A synthetic suicidal-ideation prompt produced a generic failure response, which the authors describe as an apparent crash. They recommend more detailed domestic-violence and mental-health crisis resources. Separately, five sessions contained potential personally identifiable information, including one user's full custody order across three sessions. The bot lacked meaningful information about data handling or confidentiality and did not warn against submitting personal information. The report does not claim a demonstrated data breach or assess reidentification risk.

pts.k: Maintaining a separate AI knowledge base adds operational burdens and can weaken navigation and source reliability; integration with existing court resources may work better.
pts.d: The authors identify 46 unique broken links across 97 sessions, estimate that at least 20% of knowledge-base citations appear unrelated to the answers, and find citations to multiple knowledge-base versions in 351 sessions. Some broken links arose from incorrect visible URL text despite working embedded hyperlinks, rather than necessarily being model-fabricated links. Historical website comparisons suggest that website content and the secondary knowledge base were not consistently updated together. The authors propose direct retrieval from website materials and suggest that a natural-language search interface returning relevant website results may offer a better experience and easier integration with county resources. This is a design proposal, not the result of a comparative deployment trial.

pts.k: An official court chatbot's incremental value over general-purpose AI remains an open question, including whether official status affects users' verification of answers.
pts.d: In a small comparison with GPT, Claude and Gemini, the audit team found that the Self-Help chatbot generally gave shorter, better-cited responses with more specific official-source links. General-purpose models gave more verbose answers and sometimes supplied distinctions the court chatbot omitted. For a financial-disclosure confidentiality question, only one comparison model identified a relevant 2025 law. The authors expressly decline to generalize from these tests. They raise, but do not resolve, whether widely used general-purpose tools reduce the marginal value of an official chatbot and whether users verify official-source AI answers less often.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is an exhaustive manual review of the supplied session dataset, supplemented by product inspection, historical materials and limited synthetic tests.
pts.d: The starting dataset contained 1,792 sessions. The authors received transcripts with minor redactions, answer-feedback information, historical knowledge bases and website analytics. They manually tagged every provided session, used topic-specific and fallback rubrics, and assigned impact labels to help administrators triage issues. Nearly every session had multiple reviewers, but the authors acknowledge possible inter-reader inconsistency. Overlapping topic and impact labels mean counts are not mutually exclusive and should not be treated as exact totals or aggregated into an overall harm rate. Product investigations used an open-ended snowball methodology. Additional evidence included contemporaneous synthetic prompts, small advice-boundary tests, a small foundation-model comparison, interface inspection and Internet Archive snapshots. Proposed explanations for abandonment, language barriers and retrieval failures are hypotheses rather than causal findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern this evolving Nevada product's logged 2025 use and Spring 2026 audit tests, not a forecast about all legal AI.
pts.d: The chatbot launched in summer 2024, but transcript logging began in February 2025. The Spring 2026 audit reviewed the supplied 2025 sessions and included tests in March and April 2026. Product and knowledge-base changes occurred during both the reporting and audit periods, and some recommendations may already have been implemented by publication. The authors note improvements in some areas, including an apparently fixed remote-hearing form issue in April 2026, but no observed improvement over time in emergency-custody answers. Claims about future usability and integration benefits have no quantified horizon. The report expressly confines its conclusions to the deployed product rather than general LLM suitability.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are primarily self-represented court users and the court administrators responsible for their information resources.
pts.d: Users seeking Nevada family-law and related procedural information may receive faster access to forms, explanations and court contacts, but may also encounter nonactionable answers, wrong procedures, broken links or repeated loss of conversations. Particularly relevant groups include parents in custody and support disputes, people experiencing domestic violence or mental-health crises, Spanish-speaking users, mobile users, and people sharing sensitive case information. Nevada AOC and court-resource maintainers face continuing evaluation, accessibility, safety, source-management and maintenance responsibilities. The report does not advance claims about law-firm staffing, lawyer displacement, legal-service pricing or changes to commercial legal-market structure.
